procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 21, 1967 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Revision No. 546 of 1965.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sub-Divisional Magistrate upheld a preliminary objection based on the absence of previous sanction under s. 197, Cr. P.C. The Second Additional Sessions Judge, on revision, agreed with this view. On further revision, the Patna High Court disagreed with the view taken by the two courts below and holding s. 197, Cr. P.C. to be inapplicable to the case directed the Sub-Divisional Magistrate to make further enquiry into the petition of complaint.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, Bhagwan Prasad Srivastava, assailed the view taken by the High Court. The Supreme Court granted special leave to appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complainant's case is covered by Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, making previous sanction from a superior authority necessary before the trial court can take cognizance of the complaint.

facts: The appellant, a civil surgeon, was accused in a complaint of using defamatory and abusive words against the complainant.
The appellant was also accused of having the complainant forcibly pushed out of the hospital's operation theatre by the hospital cook.
law: Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) is intended to protect public servants from frivolous or false prosecutions for offences alleged to have been committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of their official duty.
For this protection to apply, the act complained of must be directly concerned with the public servant's official duties, such that it could be claimed to have been done by virtue of the office.
The provision should not be construed too narrowly (as committing an offence is never an official duty) or too widely (as that would violate legal equality).
The key question is whether the act is directly connected to the official duty, not whether the act was a proper discharge of that duty.
application: The Court examined the specific acts alleged against the civil surgeon: using defamatory and abusive words and having the complainant forcibly removed by a cook.
It found nothing on the record to show that these actions were a part of the appellant's official duty as a Civil Surgeon.
The Court concluded that the alleged acts were not so directly connected with the performance of his official duty that he could not have properly discharged his duty without committing them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the case was not covered by Section 197 Cr.P.C. because the alleged acts of using defamatory language and having the complainant pushed out were not done in the discharge of the appellant's official duty. Therefore, previous sanction from a superior authority was not necessary for the trial court to take cognizance of the complaint.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the complainant's case is covered by Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, making previous sanction from a superior authority necessary before the trial court can take cognizance of the complaint.
appellant_arguments: The appellant, a Civil Surgeon, argued that the alleged acts (using defamatory and abusive words and having the complainant pushed out) were interrelated with his official duty and therefore attracted the protection afforded by Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, making prior sanction necessary.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the alleged offences, consisting of the use of defamatory and abusive words and being forcibly turned out of the operation theatre, were not part of the appellant's official duty as a Civil Surgeon, nor were they so directly connected with it that he could not have properly discharged his duty without committing them. Therefore, no sanction was required.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The determination of whether a public servant's act was done in the discharge of official duty, requiring prior sanction for prosecution under Section 197 Cr.P.C., is a question of fact dependent on the case's circumstances. The key consideration is not the 'duty' itself, but the 'act'; protection is granted only if the act is so directly connected with the performance of the official duty that the duty could not have been discharged without such an act.
obiter: The protection of prior sanction for prosecuting public servants should neither be too narrowly nor too widely construed.
It is no part of an official duty to commit an offence.
In our constitutional set up, the idea of legal equality or of universal subjection of all citizens to one law administered by the ordinary courts has been pushed to its utmost limits.

legal_tests_applied: The question whether ·a particular act is done by a public servant in the discharge of his official duty is substantially one of fact Jo be determined on the circumstances of each case.

It is not every offence committed by a public ·servant that requires sanction for prosecution under section 197 (I ) of the Code C·~ Criminal Procedure; nor· even every act done by him while he is actually engagr,d in the performance of his official duties; but if the act complained of is directly concerned with his official duties so that, if questicned, it c.ould he clailued to have been done by virtue of the office, then sanction wou!d be necessary.

There must be a reasonable connection between the act and the discharge of official duty; the act must bear such reiution to the duty that the accused .could lay a reasonable claim, but not a pretended or fanciful claim, that he did it in the course of the performance of his duty.

It is the quality of the act that is important and if it falls within the scope and range of the official duties of the public servant concerned the protection contemplated by s. 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code will be attracted.

policy_considerations: The object and purpose underlying section 197 Cr. P.C. is to afford protection to public servants against frivolous, vexatious or false prosecution for offences alleged to have been committed by them while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of their official duty.

The larger interest of efficiency of State administration demands that public servants should be free to perform their official duty fearlessly and undeterred by apprehension of their possible prosecution at the instance of private parties to whom annoyance or injury may have been caused by their legitimate acts done in the discharge of their official duty.

One must also guard against too wide a construction because in our constitutional set up the idea of legal equality or of universal subjection of all citizens to one law administered by the ordinary courts has been pushed to its utmost limits by enshrining equality before the law in our fundamental principles.
